headline: Bangladesh reach 96-2 at lunch in first Test against West Indies
summary: Shadman Islam remains unbeaten on 42 as the Tigers recover from an early wicket to steady their innings in Mirpur.
details: Bangladesh reached 96 for two at lunch on the opening day of the first Test against West Indies at the Sher-e-Bangla National Cricket Stadium in Mirpur.
Opener Tanzid Hasan was dismissed early for seven runs by West Indies pacer Jayden Seales, who tempted him into an edge to second slip.
The team recovered through a 59-run second-wicket partnership between Shadman Islam and Mominul Haque. Mominul contributed 28 runs before falling to Jomel Warrican.
At the lunch break, Shadman Islam remained unbeaten on 42 from 80 balls, with captain Najmul Hossain Shanto adding 15 runs in an unbroken third-wicket stand.
Captain Shanto won the toss and elected to bat first. The playing XI saw Towhid Hridoy replace the injured Mushfiqur Rahim, and Shoriful Islam replace Ebadot Hossain.
Bangladesh opted for a spin-heavy attack, retaining Mehidy Hasan Miraz, Nayeem Hasan, and Taijul Islam for the Mirpur encounter.
caption:
96-2 at lunch! 🏏 Bangladesh steadies the ship in Mirpur after an early blow.

Bangladesh reached 96 for two at lunch on the opening day of the first Test against West Indies at the Sher-e-Bangla National Cricket Stadium in Mirpur.

Opener Tanzid Hasan was dismissed early for seven runs by West Indies pacer Jayden Seales, who tempted him into an edge to second slip.

The team recovered through a 59-run second-wicket partnership between Shadman Islam and Mominul Haque. Mominul contributed 28 runs before falling to Jomel Warrican.

At the lunch break, Shadman Islam remained unbeaten on 42 from 80 balls, with captain Najmul Hossain Shanto adding 15 runs in an unbroken third-wicket stand.

Captain Shanto won the toss and elected to bat first. The playing XI saw Towhid Hridoy replace the injured Mushfiqur Rahim, and Shoriful Islam replace Ebadot Hossain.

Bangladesh opted for a spin-heavy attack, retaining Mehidy Hasan Miraz, Nayeem Hasan, and Taijul Islam for the Mirpur encounter.

headline: Deadlock in Israel: Netanyahu and rival Eisenkot both claim mandate after tight vote
summary: Exit polls show neither major bloc reached the 61-seat majority needed to govern, leaving Israel in a political stalemate following its first election since October 7.
details: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and rival Gadi Eisenkot have both vowed to form a government after a tight election where neither side secured a majority in parliament.
Exit polls indicate both the hard-right camp led by Netanyahu and the opposition bloc led by Eisenkot hold around 51 seats each, well below the 61 required to govern.
The election saw a massive voter turnout of nearly 78 percent, the highest since 1999, as citizens weighed in on Netanyahu's divisive rule and the ongoing wars.
Arab Israeli parties saw significant gains, projected to win 17 to 18 seats, driven by high turnout among minority communities protesting far-right rhetoric.
Netanyahu called for a 'strong government of the right' and suggested a third bombing campaign against Iran alongside US President Donald Trump to eliminate existential threats.
Eisenkot, a former military chief, warned Netanyahu not to use national security for political gain and called him a 'caretaker prime minister' lacking the people's trust.
Political instability remains high as far-right figures like Itamar Ben Gvir warn against a unity government, while others suggest a minority government supported by Arab lawmakers.
The deadlock occurs as Netanyahu faces an ICC arrest warrant over Gaza and domestic corruption charges that could lead to imprisonment if he loses power.
caption:
Neither side won. Israel's latest election ends in a deadlock with both Netanyahu and his rival claiming the right to lead.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and rival Gadi Eisenkot have both vowed to form a government after a tight election where neither side secured a majority in parliament.

Exit polls indicate both the hard-right camp led by Netanyahu and the opposition bloc led by Eisenkot hold around 51 seats each, well below the 61 required to govern.

The election saw a massive voter turnout of nearly 78 percent, the highest since 1999, as citizens weighed in on Netanyahu's divisive rule and the ongoing wars.

Arab Israeli parties saw significant gains, projected to win 17 to 18 seats, driven by high turnout among minority communities protesting far-right rhetoric.

Netanyahu called for a 'strong government of the right' and suggested a third bombing campaign against Iran alongside US President Donald Trump to eliminate existential threats.

Eisenkot, a former military chief, warned Netanyahu not to use national security for political gain and called him a 'caretaker prime minister' lacking the people's trust.

Political instability remains high as far-right figures like Itamar Ben Gvir warn against a unity government, while others suggest a minority government supported by Arab lawmakers.

The deadlock occurs as Netanyahu faces an ICC arrest warrant over Gaza and domestic corruption charges that could lead to imprisonment if he loses power.
